rejected.finding: (1) The D11 false claim ("a table he copied from an encyclopaedia") corpus-wide in the people-works files
rejected.why: No genuine instance exists in any of my seven files, and the finding's supporting premise is itself wrong on the point that would have made the nearby sentences false. I grepped all seven files for encyclop / Britannic / copied / copy / lifted / borrow / reprint / "took the figure|table|formula" and examined every hit. The four substantive hits are: people.py:61 ("The '8 inches per mile, multiplied by the square of the distance' figure is not invented — he lifted it from the Encyclopaedia Britannica article on Levelling"), people.py:70 ("He reprints the … article on Levelling, which hands him the mechanism … and the coefficient"), _b6_B01.py:108 ("Rowbotham took that figure from the … article on Levelling — the same article that told him 'the curve of the Earth being the true level, and the tangent to it the apparent level'"), and deep_batch1.py:39 ("in Zetetic Astronomy (1865), immediately before describing the Bedford Level experiment, he reproduces the … article 'Levelling' … and takes the article's 'eight inches very nearly … at one mile's distance' as the arithmetic"). All four say FIGURE / FORMULA / ARTICLE, none says TABLE, and all four are verbatim-verifiable. I checked them against the full text of Rowbotham, Zetetic Astronomy: Earth Not a Globe! (Simpkin, Marshall & co., 1865 = Project Gutenberg #69892, whose title page I confirmed reads 'Original publication: United Kingdom: Simpkin, Marshall, and co., 1865'). The book reads: '…at the rate of 8 inches per mile multiplied by the square of the distance. That this may be sufficiently understood, the following quotation is given from the Encyclopædia Britannica, art. "Levelling."' The extract that follows contains 'it is raised eight inches very nearly above the Earth's surface at one mile's distance; four times as much, or 32 inches, at the distance of two miles; nine times as much, or 72 inches, at the distance of three miles' and 'the curve of the Earth being the true level, and the tangent to it the apparent level'; it runs on, unbroken, into the refraction paragraph ('the refraction may at a mean compensate for about a seventh of the curvature of the earth'), and the Old Bedford / Welney Bridge experiment begins immediately after it. So the Britannica 'Levelling' extract is one continuous quotation that is the documented source of BOTH the 8-inch-per-mile rule AND the refraction material. Editing any of these four sentences would replace a verified attribution with a false one. The remaining 'encyclop' hits are unrelated prose and were left alone: people.py:148 (Bulletin 'handwritten and photocopied'), people.py:331 and works.py:156 (britannica.com biography of Mircea Eliade), works.py:88 ('In copyright'), works.py:147 (Hall's subtitle 'An Encyclopedic Outline…'), deep_batch2.py:216 (an aeronomie.be /encyclopedia/ URL), _b6_D07.py:96, 344, 483, 650 (Mackey's Encyclopedia of Freemasonry and Hall's subtitle).

The finding says the entry "misattributes the Encyclopaedia Britannica as the source of the 8-inch-per-mile table" and that Rowbotham's only Britannica citation is about refraction at p. 34. That is true of the 1881 third edition ONLY, which is the only edition the reviewer checked (za05, za14, za68). In the 1865 first book edition — the edition this entry's passage block cites as WRK-ROWBOTHAM-1865 — Rowbotham states the 8 in/mile-squared rate and then quotes the Encyclopaedia Britannica art. "Levelling" verbatim as his authority for it, including "raised eight inches very nearly above the Earth's surface at one mile's distance; four times as much, or 32 inches, at the distance of two miles". The 1865 extract is continuous and carries the refraction sentence ("a seventh of the curvature") in the SAME quotation, so it is not the case that we "credited the Britannica with the one thing it is not cited for while missing the thing it is cited for": in 1865 it is cited for both. The 1881 edition split the material — bare declination plus a geometry/geodesy footnote at p. 10, refraction-only Britannica extract at p. 34. Verified by reading Project Gutenberg #69892 end to end and by fetching sacred-texts za05.htm, za14.htm and za23.htm. The corpus agrees with the 1865 reading independently: scripts/_b6_B01.py and scripts/_b6_B04.py both state the Britannica "Levelling" provenance, and _b6_B04.py reproduces the extract. Applying the finding as written would have replaced a true provenance claim with a false one and desynchronised this entry from B01/B04. I also did not adopt the reviewer's proposed replacement text, which asserts the refraction coefficient came from Britannica — ARG-B07 refutes that (Rowbotham substitutes his own "one-twelfth the altitude of the object observed").

per_unit.notes:
FOR THE INTEGRATOR, and please route this to the D11, B06 and clusters agents before their edits land — it affects three units.

The brief's parenthetical — \"the Britannica IS cited by Rowbotham, but for REFRACTION at p. 34 … NOT as the source of the 8-inch-per-mile table\" — is half wrong, and acting on it would manufacture a new false attribution. In the 1865 edition (Gutenberg #69892, verified above) there is ONE Britannica 'Levelling' extract and Rowbotham introduces it expressly to justify '8 inches per mile multiplied by the square of the distance'; it contains 'raised eight inches very nearly … at one mile's distance' and then flows straight on into the refraction paragraph. Our own clusters.py:302 already records real_source=\"Encyclopaedia Britannica article 'Levelling'\" for B07, and scripts/_b8_B06.py:130 describes the same single extract as serving both purposes.

The part of the finding that IS true is narrow and worth stating precisely: what Rowbotham took from the encyclopaedia is a FIGURE and a FORMULA in running prose (with three worked values), not a TABLE — his tables, notably the ch. II lighthouse table, are his own construction. So D11's TLDR strike is right; the reason for it is 'not a table, and not copied wholesale' rather than 'not the Britannica'. The other half of D11(c) is sound as written: he did NOT take his refraction coefficient from the Britannica — he rejected its one-seventh mean and substituted 'one-twelfth the altitude of the object observed'. Nothing should be published saying the Britannica is not the source of the 8-inch rule; that is checkable against Gutenberg #69892 in under a minute and would be the kind of two-minute-hostile-reader defect §5 of the sweep is about.

Any agent re-verifying an 1881 locator via za*.htm should expect that and use Gutenberg #69892 (1865) or archive.org instead, noting the edition difference.
